solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Time to get in someone who'll fire supermarket employee?

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: one who fires staff is one who sacks them
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A boss summons someone with the power to sack the shelf staff at a supermarket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' suggests guns, but here it means dismissing staff; a shelf stacker fills supermarket shelves.
explanation.definitionFit: A shelf stacker is the shop worker who loads goods onto the store's shelves.

clue.text: Not working – moreover, openly gay on the street

blocks.note: a computer system that is not working is said to be down
'moreover' adds something, like 'and'
someone openly gay is out

explanation.surface: An unemployed man who is openly gay ends up homeless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not working' looks like the definition, but it supplies the first word; the definition sits at the far end.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone destitute and homeless, sleeping rough, is described as living on the street.

clue.text: Trump's way of communicating is to lose his head, babble pointlessly

indicators.note: a head is a front, so losing it means the first letter goes

blocks.note: Donald Trump famously communicated by posting on the social network

explanation.surface: A satirical jab: Trump communicates by ranting mindlessly and losing his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose his head' reads as losing his temper, but it means dropping the first letter of the social network's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To witter, a British colloquial verb, is to talk at length about trivial matters.

clue.text: Close by organ having a bad smell? Shift!

blocks.note: CL is the abbreviation for Close in British street addresses, where a close is a cul-de-sac
the ear is an organ of hearing
food that smells bad has gone off

explanation.surface: Someone standing near a stinking body part is told to move away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' is the British word for food that has spoiled and smells.
explanation.definitionFit: Shift, as a curt British command, tells someone to move away, just as the phrase tells them to leave.

clue.text: Contemptible sort of drunk protecting Johnson's butt

indicators.note: a butt is the tail end of something, so its last letter is kept
to protect is to surround and shield, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a sot is a habitual drunk
the final letter of the surname

explanation.surface: A sneer at some drunken crony who covers for Boris Johnson's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butt' looks like slang for a rear end, but it selects the last letter. Snot is British slang for a contemptible, snooty person.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a snot, in informal speech, means they are a nasty, arrogant or worthless individual.

clue.text: (& 16ac.) Grim catchphrase for the times? – "The Eye had to recruit a role model, sadly"

indicators.note: things done sadly go badly, so the letters come out in a sorry jumble

blocks.note: Private Eye refers to itself editorially as 'we'
'd is the contracted form of had
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The magazine sighs that it had to hire some role model, in grim times.
explanation.walkthrough: The magazine's 'we' plus the contraction 'd make WE'D, which joins A and ROLE MODEL as the anagram letters. The answer is written WE'RE ALL DOOMED.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is Private Frazer's gloomy catchphrase from the British sitcom Dad's Army, fitting a pessimistic era.

clue.text: Depression ought to be remedied around end of year!

indicators.note: a remedy puts something right, so these letters get fixed into a new order
the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept
around means encircling, so one piece goes about the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cry that the year-end blues should be cured.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of OUGHT are rearranged as TOUGH and placed around R.
explanation.definitionFit: A trough is a hollow or low point, so it is a depression in land, a graph or a weather map.

clue.text: Republican president's ultimately jaw-dropping tirade

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the final letter is the one taken

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
a rant is an angry tirade

explanation.surface: A Republican president ends up delivering an astonishing outburst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' looks like it means 'in the end, the president did this', but it picks the last letter of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses S. Grant, the Civil War general, served as the eighteenth United States president for the Republican Party.

clue.text: Force instrument on Trump's powerless sidekick

indicators.note: power is abbreviated P, so being without power means that letter is dropped

blocks.note: a viol is an old stringed instrument
names whose sidekick is meant; it supplies no letters of its own
Trump's sidekick was his vice-president, Mike Pence

explanation.surface: Someone forces an instrument on Trump's weak deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' looks like a verb, but it is the noun definition. In an across clue, 'on' means one piece follows the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Violence is physical force used to hurt or damage, so the two nouns are near synonyms.

clue.text: Crazy lays on the rise over one day

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to lay something down is to put it
I is the Roman numeral for one
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A mad tale of hens whose laying is increasing over a single day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lays' suggests eggs, but it is the verb meaning puts; in a down clue, 'over' places it above what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazy and stupid are both informal ways of calling an idea or person foolish or senseless.

clue.text: Get hold of jailbird – time to do something

blocks.note: a con is a convict
T is the abbreviation for time
to act is to do something

explanation.surface: A call to seize an escaped prisoner: it's time for action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get hold of' sounds like arresting the jailbird, but it means reaching someone by phone or message.
explanation.definitionFit: To get hold of someone, in everyday speech, is to reach them by phone or message.

clue.text: White wine in extremity and a snack

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside another

blocks.note: a toe is at the extremity of the foot
Asti is a sparkling white wine from Piedmont

explanation.surface: A desperate moment calls for white wine and something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In extremity' reads as an idiom for desperate straits, but 'in' is the container signal and 'extremity' a body part. A toastie is British slang for a toasted sandwich.
explanation.definitionFit: A toastie is a toasted sandwich, a quick light bite eaten between meals.

clue.text: Artist set out to be probed by a lot of sailors

indicators.note: laid out afresh, these letters take a new arrangement
a probe goes inside something, so one piece is entered by the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the Royal Navy, abbreviated RN, is a large body of sailors

explanation.surface: A painter sets off only to be interrogated by a crowd of seamen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' looks like a phrasal verb meaning departed; 'out' is the anagram signal for SET alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Ernst was a German painter and a leading figure of the Dada and Surrealist movements.

clue.text: Staff roles Penn ballsed up

indicators.note: something ballsed up is badly bungled, so these letters end up in a mess

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A manager called Penn botched the assignment of jobs to employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ballsed up' is vulgar British slang for messed up, a typical Private Eye anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Personnel are the people employed by an organisation, so the word is a synonym for its workforce.

clue.text: Business-like, but lacking balls

blocks.note: lacking something means having none of it
balls is British slang for rubbish talk

explanation.surface: Someone is efficient, but cowardly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking balls' reads as lacking courage; balls here is British slang for nonsense, so the phrase means free of nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: A brisk, efficient, practical manner is described as businesslike or no-nonsense in everyday usage.

clue.text: see 6dn.
Showing virtue, I'm about to entertain a sort of sex with politician – no alternative

definitions.note: a phrase describing conduct, used here as the noun for virtuous behaviour

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
to entertain a guest is to have them inside, so one piece holds another
'no' means without, so the following letters are removed

blocks.note: taken as written
oral is a sort of sex
a Tory is a British Conservative politician
'or' introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A virtuous claimant admits planning a sexual encounter with a politician, having no choice.
explanation.walkthrough: MI holds ORAL, then TORY loses OR to leave TY. A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Morality is the quality of behaving rightly, so displaying it means acting with virtue and good principle.

clue.text: Bad tip: do something criminal

blocks.note: food gone bad is off
a tip is an end

explanation.surface: A dodgy piece of advice: go and break the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' suggests advice, but it means the end of something.
explanation.definitionFit: To offend, in legal language, is to commit a crime or break the law.

clue.text: Be preoccupied with love and Elizabeth I having sex

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
Good Queen Bess was the nickname of Elizabeth I
S is an abbreviation for sex

explanation.surface: A historian fixates on romance and the Virgin Queen's sex life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' joins the love to the queen, and the queen's nickname takes S after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To obsess is to have one's mind continually filled with a single thing, so it means being preoccupied.

clue.text: Complaint: "Isn't getting stuffed by Mel awful?"

indicators.note: something awful is in a bad state, so these letters are jumbled
being stuffed means being filled, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: ain't is a colloquial form of isn't
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about how dreadful it is being cheated by a man named Mel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' sounds like a grumble, introduced by the colon, but it is a medical complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint, in the medical sense, is an illness or disorder, which is exactly what an ailment is.

clue.text: Animal dropping expression, endlessly broadcast

indicators.note: without an end, the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: scat is the dung of a wild animal
a term is a word or expression

explanation.surface: A phrase about animal mess keeps being aired on radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' suggests radio, but its older sense is sowing seed by flinging it widely.
explanation.definitionFit: To broadcast seed is to scatter it by hand over a wide area, the farming origin of the word.

clue.text: Concerns pisspoor street in Scotland's capital

indicators.note: something pisspoor is shoddily made, so these letters come out jumbled
a capital is the head letter of a word, so the first is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Worries about a run-down road in Edinburgh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotland's capital' wants to be Edinburgh; it is just the first letter. 'In' looks like a link but joins the anagram letters.
explanation.definitionFit: One's concerns are the matters one cares about or has a stake in, in other words one's interests.

clue.text: I'd backed away from neighbourhood disciplinarian

definitions.note: a noun in the clue, used for the adjective describing such a person

indicators.note: going backwards means the letters are read in the opposite order
being away from something means taken out of it, so letters are removed

blocks.note: taken as written
a district is a neighbourhood

explanation.surface: Someone says they retreated from a local enforcer of rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed away' looks like one phrase meaning retreated, but 'backed' reverses and 'away from' removes.
explanation.definitionFit: A disciplinarian enforces rules firmly, which is the quality of being strict in behaviour.

clue.text: see 25dn.
City partly responsible for zipper thongs

indicators.note: partly means only in part, so the answer is a piece of the words that follow

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A city takes some blame for skimpy zipped underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partly responsible' looks like one phrase about blame; 'partly' alone signals the hidden word.
explanation.definitionFit: Perth is a city, both the capital of Western Australia and a Scottish city on the Tay.

clue.text: One who'd stick nose in fruity thing, it's said

indicators.note: what is said is spoken, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: a medlar is a brown fruit eaten when nearly rotten

explanation.surface: A nosy person poking around in some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick nose in' first suggests sniffing fruit; together with 'One who'd' it means a busybody.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sticks their nose in interferes in other people's business, the idiom for being nosy.

clue.text: (& 23ac.) Pandemic to end badly? Deem unnecessary and keep cool

indicators.note: what is unnecessary can be left out, so those letters are removed
done poorly, the letters land in a muddled order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, then removed

explanation.surface: Will the pandemic end badly? Consider it needless worry and stay calm.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of DEEM out of PANDEMIC TO END and rearrange the rest. The answer is written DON'T PANIC.
explanation.definitionFit: The command urges someone to stay calm in a crisis, the same advice as keeping cool.

clue.text: A bellyful of froth and sex without energy

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense means outside, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: surf is the froth of breaking waves
E is the symbol for energy
'it' is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: Someone has had enough of fluffy fun and listless sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but here it means outside, so the froth and the sex sit either side of E.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellyful is more than enough of something, which is what a surfeit, an excess, means.

clue.text: Clegg about on street? Won't hold!

definitions.note: a verb phrase in the clue, describing what the adjective's surface does

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece is placed around the rest

blocks.note: Nick Clegg was the Liberal Democrat leader
taken as written
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg out campaigning in the street — and nothing he says will stick.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Clegg led Britain's Liberal Democrats and was deputy prime minister from 2010 to 2015.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-stick pan has a coating that food will not adhere to, so it won't hold anything.

clue.text: Pure heroin included in order

indicators.note: being included in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: H is slang for heroin
a caste is a social order or class

explanation.surface: Uncut heroin being part of a drug order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pure heroin' reads as one drug phrase; 'Pure' is the definition and the heroin is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste means sexually virtuous and morally clean, a standard sense of the adjective pure.
